title: Sesshin
hookLine: days of intensive silent sitting in a Zen monastery or center
last: A KOAN OR JUST SITTING: TWO DOORS, ONE HOUSE.

cards: Before dawn, a wooden clapper sounds down a dark hallway. People roll up their bedding without a word and file into the meditation hall. Shoes in a row by the door, cushions in a row along the wall.

Breakfast is eaten in silence, and so is lunch, and so is the walk back to the hall. Not for an hour, but for days. In Zen monasteries and in Zen centers in ordinary towns, this stretch of time has a name.

teach.b: First, the word. Sesshin is Japanese, often rendered as gathering the mind, or touching the mind.
Picture water spread thin across a table, drawn together into one bowl: attention usually scattered across a day, collected in one place. Second, the shape of a day.
Mostly zazen, sitting, in periods marked by a bell, with slow walking between. There are chants, meals, a period of work and a talk from the teacher.

teach.h: FORMS SO NO ONE HAS TO DECIDE.
teach.b: Tradition fills the gaps with forms: when to bow, where to put your bowl, how to enter the hall. They aren't there to make it hard; they're there so nobody has to decide anything, and the mind has fewer places to run.
Third, the silence. Participants don't talk, and some keep their eyes lowered. Some describe the first day or two as the loudest part: the silence outside lets every thought inside be heard.
Both schools you met yesterday hold sesshin. A Rinzai one may lean on koan work and meetings with the teacher; a Soto one may lean on just sitting.
An evening sit is a single drop of water on a stone. Days of sitting give the mind time to settle in a way one short sit rarely can. Then it ends.
People bow, speak their first words, and go home to traffic and email, bringing back not the silence itself but a memory of what a gathered mind is like.

how: Zen monasteries and many Zen centers hold sesshin, retreats of several days in which participants keep silence and follow a fixed schedule of sitting, walking meditation, chanting, work, meals and talks from the teacher.

o: a vow of lifelong silence taken by Zen monastics
days of silent, intensive Zen practice, the mind gathered
a single evening of quiet sitting at a local temple

s: sesshin is a single long sitting with no breaks
the days mix sitting with walking, chanting, meals, work and a teacher's talk.
both Rinzai and Soto teachers hold sesshin
the emphasis may differ, koans in one, just sitting in the other, but each holds sesshin.
the silence is kept even at meals
meals are eaten in silence too.

games.q: it's the first full day of sesshin. the hall is silent, but your mind is louder than it has been in months. what does this mean?
o: you're doing it wrong and should leave.
it's common: outer silence lets inner noise be heard.
you should start talking to quiet it.
games.why: some who sit sesshin describe the first day or two as the loudest. the days that follow give it time to settle.

practice: Picture one day of sesshin as if you were there: the clapper before dawn, your cushion in its row, breathing in silence beside people whose names you may not know.
Then let the picture go, and notice that in this small sit you're doing the same thing they do. When the mind scatters, gather it back to one breath.

wordCard.voice: Sesshin. Days of silent, intensive practice in a Zen monastery or center: sitting, walking, eating and working, with the mind gathered in one place. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: sesshin, rendered 'gathering' or 'touching' the mind. some communities write it 摂心.

carryVoice: Your line: gathering the mind. Scattered water, drawn together into one bowl. The week closes here.

sources.work: Zen communal practice, Rinzai and Soto
